name: Febrile Seizures
overview: Convulsions or seizures in infants and young children (aged 6 months to 5 years) triggered by a rapid spike in body temperature, usually from a common viral infection.
summary: Convulsions or seizures in infants and young children (aged 6 months to 5 years) triggered by a rapid spike in body temperature, usually from a common viral infection.

Immature developing central nervous system with lower seizure threshold

symptoms: Sudden loss of consciousness during high fever
Rhythmic jerking or twitching movements of both arms and legs
Eyes rolling upward or staring blankly
Body becomes stiff and rigid
Breathing becomes irregular or shallow; lips may look slightly dark
Brief duration: usually lasts less than 2-3 minutes, followed by drowsiness (post-ictal sleep)

reports_tests.normal_range: Normal neurological examination, child returns to baseline
reports_tests.explanation: Simple febrile seizure: generalized, lasts < 15 mins, does not recur within 24 hours; Complex: focal, > 15 mins, or repeats in 24 hours
Rules out hypoglycemia or electrolyte disturbance provoking seizures
Mandatory if signs of meningitis (bulging fontanelle, stiff neck, persistent lethargy) are present

treatment: Emergency First Aid: Place child on their side in recovery position, protect head, time the seizure, NEVER put anything in mouth; Rectal Diazepam or intranasal Midazolam if seizure lasts > 5 minutes; Antipyretics (Paracetamol) to lower temperature for comfort; Reassurance (febrile seizures do NOT cause brain damage).
diet_lifestyle: First Aid During Seizure: Gently turn child onto their SIDE (recovery position) so saliva can drain out and tongue doesn't block airway; Protect child from hard furniture; Loosen tight clothing around neck; NEVER put your fingers, keys, or spoons inside their mouth; NEVER hold their limbs down to stop jerking

Give prescribed paracetamol when child has fever, but understand that fever medicines do not reliably prevent febrile seizures
emergency_signs: Seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes, seizure affecting only one side of the body, child does not wake up or recognize you within 30 minutes, or child has a stiff neck (Call 108 immediately)

summary: Skeletal disorder in growing infants and children caused by severe Vitamin D and calcium deficiency, leading to soft, weak bones that bend under body weight.

overview: Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children resulting from inadequate intake of calories, proteins, and essential micronutrients, presenting as Marasmus (severe wasting) or Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency with edema).
summary: Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children resulting from inadequate intake of calories, proteins, and essential micronutrients, presenting as Marasmus (severe wasting) or Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency with edema).

Early cessation of breastfeeding followed by dilute unhygienic animal milk
Recurrent diarrheal illnesses and intestinal worm infestations

name: Dengue Fever
overview: Mosquito-borne tropical viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV 1-4), transmitted by day-biting Aedes mosquitoes, known as 'breakbone fever'.
summary: Mosquito-borne tropical viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV 1-4), transmitted by day-biting Aedes mosquitoes, known as 'breakbone fever'.

However, it is 100% PREVENTABLE if Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) is started IMMEDIATELY after animal exposure: 1. Immediate wound washing with soap and running water for 15 minutes, 2. Rabies Vaccine (Intramuscular on days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28), 3. Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) infiltrated into Category III bite wounds.

Apply povidone iodine or alcohol antiseptic to the wound
DO NOT cover the wound with bandages, and NEVER suture (stitch) the bite wound initially

name: Tetanus (Lockjaw)
overview: Severe, potentially fatal neurological disease caused by the neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani bacteria, entering the body through wounds contaminated with soil, dung, or rusty metal.
summary: Severe, potentially fatal neurological disease caused by the neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani bacteria, entering the body through wounds contaminated with soil, dung, or rusty metal.
causes: Clostridium tetani bacterial spores entering wounds through deep puncture wounds (stepping on rusty nails), animal bites, open fractures, burns, or contaminated surgical/umbilical cutting instruments
symptoms: Trismus ('lockjaw'): Severe, painful spasm of the jaw muscles making it impossible to open the mouth
Risus sardonicus: Fixed, unnatural grimacing smile caused by facial muscle spasms
Opisthotonos: Severe, painful, arching muscle spasms of the back and neck (body arches backward like a bow)
Violent, painful generalized muscle spasms triggered by sudden minor stimuli like noise, bright light, or touch
warning_signs: Trismus ('lockjaw'): Severe, painful spasm of the jaw muscles making it impossible to open the mouth
Risus sardonicus: Fixed, unnatural grimacing smile caused by facial muscle spasms
Opisthotonos: Severe, painful, arching muscle spasms of the back and neck (body arches backward like a bow)
Violent, painful generalized muscle spasms triggered by sudden minor stimuli like noise, bright light, or touch

reports_tests.explanation: Bedside clinical test: touching posterior pharyngeal wall with a tongue depressor causes involuntary jaw clamping (positive in 94% of tetanus)
Diagnosis is strictly clinical; bacterial cultures from wounds are positive in only 30% of cases

treatment: Emergency intensive care: Human Tetanus Immunoglobulin (HTIG) to neutralize unbound toxin, aggressive wound debridement, IV antibiotics (Metronidazole), muscle relaxants and sedation (Benzodiazepines, Vecuronium), tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation in quiet dark ICU room.
diet_lifestyle: Clean and wash all dirty cuts, scrapes, and puncture wounds thoroughly with soap and water immediately
Keep the patient in a quiet, dark, peaceful hospital room to avoid triggering violent muscular spasms
Patients who survive tetanus do NOT develop natural immunity; a full vaccination course is mandatory

prevention: Ensure up-to-date Tetanus Toxoid (TT / Td) vaccination every 10 years throughout adulthood, and a booster within 48 hours of any dirty wound

name: Leptospirosis (Rat Fever)
overview: Bacterial zoonotic infection caused by Leptospira bacteria, transmitted through contact with water or soil contaminated with the urine of infected animals (especially rats during monsoon floods).
summary: Bacterial zoonotic infection caused by Leptospira bacteria, transmitted through contact with water or soil contaminated with the urine of infected animals (especially rats during monsoon floods).
causes: Walking or wading through floodwaters contaminated with rat or rodent urine (common during monsoon flooding)
Skin cuts, abrasions, or mucous membranes coming into contact with contaminated water, mud, or sewage
Agricultural workers, sanitation workers, and rice paddy farmers
symptoms: Biphasic illness: 1. Septicemic phase: Sudden high fever, severe frontal headache, intense muscle tenderness (characteristically in the calves and lower back), and conjunctival suffusion (prominent red eyes WITHOUT pus or discharge)
2. Immune phase (Weil's disease): Jaundice, acute kidney failure (oliguria), bleeding, and pulmonary hemorrhage
warning_signs: Biphasic illness: 1. Septicemic phase: Sudden high fever, severe frontal headache, intense muscle tenderness (characteristically in the calves and lower back), and conjunctival suffusion (prominent red eyes WITHOUT pus or discharge)

reports_tests.explanation: Gold standard serological test: 4-fold rise in MAT antibody titer between acute and convalescent sera

reports_tests.test: Leptospira IgM ELISA / Rapid Card Test
reports_tests.explanation: Rapid screening serology detectable from day 5-7 of illness
Monitors development of acute renal failure and direct hyperbilirubinemia in severe Weil's syndrome

treatment: Early antibiotic therapy: Oral Doxycycline (100mg twice daily for 7 days) for mild disease; Intravenous crystalline Penicillin G or Ceftriaxone for severe Weil's disease; Hemodialysis for acute renal failure; Mechanical ventilation for pulmonary hemorrhage.
diet_lifestyle: NEVER wade or walk barefoot through monsoon floodwaters, waterlogged streets, or stagnant drains
Wear high rubber gumboots and waterproof gloves if working in muddy fields or flood relief work
Wash feet and legs thoroughly with soap and clean water immediately after any flood contact

prevention: Prophylactic Doxycycline (200mg single weekly dose) recommended for high-risk workers during active flood relief operations

name: Scrub Typhus
overview: Acute febrile illness caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi, transmitted to humans through the bite of infected larval trombiculid mites ('chiggers') in grassy bush areas.
summary: Acute febrile illness caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi, transmitted to humans through the bite of infected larval trombiculid mites ('chiggers') in grassy bush areas.
causes: Bite of microscopic chigger mites in overgrown bushes, grass, and agricultural fields
Walking or working in rural farmland, jungles, or overgrown gardens
Peak incidence during rainy and post-monsoon months
symptoms: Sudden high spiking fever and severe chills
Severe headache, body aches, and dry cough
Pathognomonic 'ESCHAR': A painless, black, cigarette-burn-like necrotic scab with an erythematous halo at the site of the chigger bite (often hidden in groin, armpits, or waist)
Swollen lymph nodes and a generalized flat red rash

Traditional screening test: significant agglutination with Proteus OX-K antigen supports diagnosis

Wear long trousers tucked into socks and long-sleeved shirts when walking in tall grass or farmland
Apply permethrin or DEET insect repellent to clothes and shoes

name: Amoebiasis (Amoebic Dysentery & Liver Abscess)
overview: Parasitic infection caused by the protozoan Entamoeba histolytica, causing intestinal ulceration (amoebic dysentery with bloody diarrhea) or spread to the liver (amoebic liver abscess).
summary: Parasitic infection caused by the protozoan Entamoeba histolytica, causing intestinal ulceration (amoebic dysentery with bloody diarrhea) or spread to the liver (amoebic liver abscess).
causes: Ingestion of mature Entamoeba histolytica cysts in fecally contaminated food or drinking water
Eating raw street salads or fruits washed in unboiled water
Poor personal hand hygiene and open defecation
symptoms: Intestinal Dysentery: Frequent, small-volume loose stools mixed with dark blood and abundant mucus, severe lower abdominal cramping and pain, tenesmus (painful straining to pass stool)
Amoebic Liver Abscess: High fever with chills, constant dull aching pain in the upper right abdomen, pain radiating to the right shoulder, and enlarged tender liver
warning_signs: Intestinal Dysentery: Frequent, small-volume loose stools mixed with dark blood and abundant mucus, severe lower abdominal cramping and pain, tenesmus (painful straining to pass stool)

reports_tests.explanation: Identifies active motile Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis)
Demonstrates solitary, round, hypoechoic abscess cavity (characteristically in the right lobe, containing 'anchovy sauce' thick pus)
Positive in > 95% of patients with amoebic liver abscess

treatment: Tissue amoebicide: Oral Metronidazole (400-800mg 3x daily for 7-10 days) or Tinidazole; followed by Luminal amoebicide: Diloxanide furoate or Paromomycin to eradicate dormant cysts in the bowel; Needle aspiration under ultrasound for large liver abscesses risking rupture.
diet_lifestyle: Drink only boiled or filtered water (ordinary chemical water purification may not reliably kill thick-walled amoebic cysts; boiling water kills cysts)
Peel all fresh fruits yourself and avoid raw street salads
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water after using the toilet

name: H1N1 Influenza (Swine Flu)
overview: Acute respiratory viral infection caused by the Influenza A H1N1 virus strain, spreading rapidly through droplets and causing high fever, cough, and potential viral pneumonia.
summary: Acute respiratory viral infection caused by the Influenza A H1N1 virus strain, spreading rapidly through droplets and causing high fever, cough, and potential viral pneumonia.

Touching surfaces contaminated with flu virus and then touching eyes, nose, or mouth
Crowded public transit and seasonal winter spikes

Severe dry, persistent hacking cough and sore throat
Intense, deep muscle and body aches (myalgia) and severe fatigue

Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea in some patients

Wash hands with soap and water frequently

name: HIV / AIDS
overview: Human Immunodeficiency Virus infection that attacks the body's immune system, specifically destroying CD4 T-lymphocytes, leading to Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) if untreated.
summary: Human Immunodeficiency Virus infection that attacks the body's immune system, specifically destroying CD4 T-lymphocytes, leading to Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) if untreated.
causes: Unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected partner
Sharing needles, syringes, or drug equipment
Transfusion of unscreened blood or blood products
Mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding
Accidental needlestick injuries in healthcare workers
symptoms: Acute primary infection (2-4 weeks): Mononucleosis-like flu, fever, rash, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes
Chronic latent stage: Often asymptomatic for 5-10 years

Advanced AIDS: Drenching night sweats, persistent unexplained diarrhea > 1 month, dramatic rapid weight loss ('wasting syndrome'), chronic oral fungal thrush, recurrent opportunistic infections (TB, Pneumocystis pneumonia)

reports_tests.normal_range: Non-reactive for HIV-1/2 antibodies and p24 antigen
reports_tests.explanation: Standard 3-test screening strategy under India's National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO)
Measures immune competence: levels < 200 cells/mcL defines AIDS and high vulnerability to opportunistic infections
Monitors success of antiretroviral therapy: Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U)

Eat a balanced nutritious diet and drink clean boiled water

overview: Slow, progressive parasitic disease caused by Leishmania donovani protozoa, transmitted through the bites of infected female phlebotomine sandflies.

Endemic in rural eastern India (Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, eastern UP)
symptoms: Prolonged, irregular, recurrent fever lasting weeks to months
Massive enlargement of the spleen (splenomegaly, belly becomes enlarged and firm)
Severe progressive weight loss, weakness, and emaciation
Progressive darkening or grayish-black pigmentation of the skin of hands, feet, and abdomen (giving the disease its name 'Kala-Azar' / Black Fever)

name: Filariasis (Elephantiasis)
overview: Chronic parasitic infection caused by microscopic filarial nematode worms transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, leading to irreversible lymphedema and massive swelling of limbs.
summary: Chronic parasitic infection caused by microscopic filarial nematode worms transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, leading to irreversible lymphedema and massive swelling of limbs.
causes: Infection with Wuchereria bancrofti filarial worms (causes 98% of cases in India)
Bite of infected Culex quinquefasciatus mosquitoes (breeds in dirty, stagnant drains and sewage)
Adult worms lodge and live inside human lymphatic vessels for 6-8 years, causing chronic lymphatic damage
symptoms: Acute adenolymphangitis (ADL) attacks: Episodic high fever, chills, and painful red swelling spreading down the leg or arm

Chyluria (passing milky white urine containing lymph fluid)

name: Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome
overview: Neuropsychiatric emergency caused by severe thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, common in chronic alcoholism and malnutrition, characterized by acute encephalopathy (Wernicke's) followed by irreversible anterograde memory loss (Korsakoff's).
summary: Neuropsychiatric emergency caused by severe thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, common in chronic alcoholism and malnutrition, characterized by acute encephalopathy (Wernicke's) followed by irreversible anterograde memory loss (Korsakoff's).

Poor dietary intake combined with impaired intestinal thiamine absorption and reduced liver storage
Giving IV glucose/dextrose to a malnourished alcoholic WITHOUT prior thiamine administration

Korsakoff's Syndrome (chronic phase): Severe anterograde amnesia (complete inability to form any new memories), retrograde memory loss, and Confabulation (inventing plausible stories to cover up memory gaps without realizing they are fabricated)

overview: Malignant tumor arising from the lining of the stomach (most commonly gastric adenocarcinoma), often diagnosed at an advanced stage due to non-specific early symptoms.
summary: Malignant tumor arising from the lining of the stomach (most commonly gastric adenocarcinoma), often diagnosed at an advanced stage due to non-specific early symptoms.

Chronic atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia

Unexplained weight loss and profound loss of appetite
Vomiting blood (hematemesis) or passing dark black tarry stools (melena)
Palpable hard lymph node above the left collarbone (Virchow's node)

overview: Malignant tumor that forms in the tissues of the prostate gland in men, one of the most common cancers in aging men, often slow-growing initially.
summary: Malignant tumor that forms in the tissues of the prostate gland in men, one of the most common cancers in aging men, often slow-growing initially.

overview: Malignant cancer of the blood and bone marrow, characterized by rapid, uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal, immature white blood cells (blasts) that crowd out healthy cells.
summary: Malignant cancer of the blood and bone marrow, characterized by rapid, uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal, immature white blood cells (blasts) that crowd out healthy cells.

Exposure to ionizing radiation and benzene chemicals

Frequent, recurrent, or persistent infections and fever (defective white blood cells)
Easy bruising (ecchymoses), tiny pinpoint red/purple spots on skin (petechiae), and spontaneous bleeding from gums or nose (thrombocytopenia)
